title: Microsoft Japanese Style Guide
rule: Body text, dialogs, messages use desu-masu (polite); prompts to act use 'shite kudasai'; titles and command buttons use noun phrases (taigen-dome). Do not use honorific (sonkeigo) or humble (kenjogo) forms in general. Avoid written-language/very formal words; the voice avoids unnecessary formality.
example: Button: noun phrase; message: ...してください。

title: Microsoft Japanese Style Guide (second person)
rule: Second person is often omitted. When needed, name the role (ユーザー, 管理者); お客様 or ご自分 in customer-sensitive text; 'あなた' only after asking whether it is needed and whether it sounds impolite. Strict word-for-word translation makes tone stiff; 'we' as 弊社 only when very polite or official.
example: ユーザー / 管理者 / お客様 instead of translating 'you'
llm_tell: Carrying the English 'you' over as あなた in every sentence reads as translated text (inference from the guide's own warning, not measured).

title: Microsoft German Style Guide
rule: Address the user with formal Sie, with first/second person ('wir', 'Sie') in place of abstract 'Benutzer' (impersonal references sound formal; 'wir' suggests a team that cares, but check context, it can sound odd in German). For under-18s use informal du. Prefer active voice with imperative or indicative over subjunctive or passive, which sound formal. Use German quotes „ “ and Gedankenstrich (en dash).
example: 'Benutzer können den Zeitpunkt festlegen' -> 'Sie bestimmen, wann neue Updates installiert werden sollen.'

title: Microsoft Spanish (Neutral) Style Guide
rule: Tu/usted is a per-product decision (Office, Exchange, Dynamics: usted; Skype, Store, Windows Phone: tu); the modern voice recommends informal tu, plural 'ustedes' not 'vosotros'. Prefer impersonal forms over repeating 'tu' in every sentence. Keep opening ¿ and ¡. Adjectives of nationality are not capitalized (unlike English).
example: 'Operation failed!' -> 'No se pudo realizar la operación.' (impersonal, no exclamation)

title: W3C: Personal names around the world
topic: Names and forms of address across cultures
rule: Family-name-first in Japan, Korea, Hungary (and China). Spanish names carry two family names; Brazilian up to four; Russians use given-patronymic-family. Do not require a family name (many in Southern India, Malaysia, Indonesia have one name); avoid 'first/last name' labels; preserve case entered; allow spaces. Given-name address can imply prior acquaintance; titles matter in Germany; adding an honorific is normal in Japan; ask the user how they want to be addressed rather than assume.
example: Icelanders prefer the given name even with strangers; Germans expect titles.
llm_tell: Defaulting to 'Dear Mr. [Last name]' or 'Hi [First name]' by US pattern, and splitting every name into first/last (inference).

title: Microsoft Localization Style Guides index
rule: Microsoft publishes a style guide per locale (about 100, including es-ES/es-MX/es-US/es-neutral, fr-FR vs fr-CA, pt-BR vs pt-PT). Each fixes address form, tone, punctuation and terminology for that market, so register is a per-market decision, not per language. aka.ms/<language>-styleguide redirects to a PDF.

title: Distinguishing ChatGPT(-3.5, -4)-generated and human-written papers through Japanese stylometric analysis (Zaitsu & Jin, PLOS ONE 2023)
rule: On 72 human papers vs 72 each GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, function-word rate separated best (98.1% random forest); comma placement 93.5% (top variable: comma right after は); POS bigrams 95.4% (top: noun + particle); particle bigrams worst 92.6% (top: が+が). Direction of each difference is not reported in the paper. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 overlapped. Authors conclude humans cannot reliably tell them apart. Not studied: kanji/hiragana.
llm_tell: Japanese LLM text differs in function-word rate, comma placement after は, and particle sequences; invisible to readers, visible to classifiers (academic papers only).

title: Do Large Language Models Have an English Accent? Evaluating and Improving the Naturalness of Multilingual LLMs (Guo et al.)
rule: Corpus-level lexical and syntactic naturalness metrics show LLM output in French and Chinese leans toward English-influenced patterns in vocabulary and grammar; an alignment method improved naturalness without hurting general benchmarks. Per-language numbers not read.
llm_tell: Non-English output carries English syntax and word choice (an English accent); a native reader hears it as translated.

title: How Close is ChatGPT to Human Experts? (HC3, Guo et al. 2023)
rule: On 12,853 Chinese questions, ChatGPT answers were longer (about twice in open_qa and medical splits) with a smaller vocabulary; human answers were shorter with higher word density in every split. Question-answer text, ChatGPT of early 2023.
llm_tell: Longer, lexically narrower Chinese answers than a human gives.

title: Cultural determinants of email communication styles (Holtbruegge, Weldon, Rogers 2013), via search summary
rule: Cultural background significantly affects preferences for formality, promptness, preciseness, task-relatedness and relationship-relatedness in email. Specifics per culture not read.

title: Skalski, student thesis on German, American, Japanese email (via search summary)
rule: Summarising earlier literature: Americans and Japanese sit at opposite ends of directness; Germans more direct than Americans, which others may judge negatively; Japanese address forms mirror hierarchy; American first-name use does not signal intimacy. A thesis, secondhand, no new corpus.
llm_tell: A single warm, hedged American-friendly email template sent to every culture (inference).

title: Zulip German translation guide, via search summary
rule: Zulip's German guide recommends informal du for a chat product and anglicisms only if other web apps use them; Microsoft's Windows voice uses Sie. The choice follows the product, not the language.
